title: ABDON HAD FORTY SONS AND THIRTY GRANDSONS—WHAT DO THESE ENORMOUS JUDGE-ERA FAMILIES TELL US?
paragraphs: ABDON HAD FORTY SONS AND THIRTY GRANDSONS—WHAT DO THESE ENORMOUS JUDGE-ERA FAMILIES TELL US?

Seventy descendants. Seventy donkeys. Eight years of leadership. Three verses. And buried inside this almost-forgotten judge’s story is a warning about success, legacy, family, influence—and the one thing none of them can save.
There are Bible verses we underline.
There are verses we preach from pulpits, print on coffee mugs, write inside birthday cards, and whisper through tears when life collapses.
And then there are verses like Judges 12:13–15.
We encounter a collection of numbers.
But maybe we are moving too fast.

Because Scripture suddenly introduces a man named Abdon, gives us only a few sentences about his life, surrounds him with an enormous family, tells us that seventy of his descendants rode seventy donkeys, tells us that he judged Israel for eight years...
and then tells us he died.
Listen carefully, because what looks like an obscure genealogy may force you to ask one of the most uncomfortable questions a human being can face:
If God wrote only three verses about your life, what would actually matter enough to remain?
The Hebrew text of Judges 12:14 reads:
וַיְהִי־לוֹ אַרְבָּעִים בָּנִים וּשְׁלֹשִׁים בְּנֵי בָנִים רֹכְבִים עַל־שִׁבְעִים עֲיָרִם וַיִּשְׁפֹּט אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל שְׁמֹנֶה שָׁנִים
Vayehi-lo arba'im banim u-sheloshim benei vanim, rokhevim al-shiv'im ayarim; vayishpot et-Yisrael shemoneh shanim.
“He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode on seventy donkeys, and he judged Israel eight years.”
And Abdon was not the only judge whose family size receives unusual attention.
Just a few verses earlier, Ibzan is described as having thirty sons and thirty daughters. Earlier still, Jair had thirty sons who rode thirty donkeys and controlled thirty towns.
This means the detail concerning Abdon is not floating alone in the book.
The Bible does not explicitly tell us, “Abdon's seventy descendants prove this exact sociological theory.” We should never make Scripture say what Scripture does not say.
But the details are clearly important enough for the inspired narrator to preserve them.

And within Judges itself, riding donkeys appears elsewhere alongside people of standing. Judges 5:10 addresses those who ride on white donkeys, while Judges 10:4 describes Jair's thirty sons riding thirty donkeys.
So when Abdon appears with forty sons, thirty grandsons, and seventy donkey-riding descendants, we are not being shown the portrait of an isolated, powerless man.
We are looking at a substantial household.
A man whose influence had multiplied across generations.
Not forty names printed in a genealogy.
Thirty grandsons growing up underneath the shadow of the family name.
A household large enough that wherever the family went, people probably noticed.
And at the center of it all stood Abdon.
For most of us, seventy direct male descendants sounds almost unimaginable.
We live in an age where getting four relatives into the same photograph can feel like a military operation.
Abdon had forty sons and thirty grandsons recorded in Scripture.
But here is where this little passage begins to hurt.
after eight years of judging Israel...
Judges 12:15 essentially brings the curtain down:
An entire human empire reduced to a grave.
And the Bible loves us too much to let us pretend mortality belongs only to somebody else.
You can have children who carry your name.
You can become the person everyone calls when something goes wrong.
You can accumulate achievements until your biography sounds extraordinary.
someone else will carry your body.
Someone else will close the door to your house.
Someone else will sit in your chair.
Someone else will inherit things you spent decades acquiring.
And eventually people who never met you will walk past the place where you were buried.
That is why Abdon's seventy descendants should not merely make us curious about ancient families.
They should make us think about ours.
Some parents are working themselves nearly to death to give their children everything except the one treasure their children desperately need.
We worry about what school they attend, what career they choose, what house they eventually own, and whether they will be financially comfortable.
But somewhere between paying bills and planning futures, it is frighteningly possible to raise children who know how to survive in this world but do not know the Savior who can rescue them from sin.
Imagine leaving your child property but no prayer life.
Money but no knowledge of Scripture.
A family name but no understanding of the name above every name.
A Christian label but no love for Christ.
What good is an impressive family tree if its branches grow farther and farther away from God?
This is where we must resist another temptation.
Judges 12 does not tell us the spiritual condition of Abdon's forty sons and thirty grandsons.
We cannot honestly preach that they were righteous.
We cannot honestly preach that they were wicked.
The text does not tell us.
And perhaps that silence itself should humble us.
Because Scripture tells us what they rode...
but does not give us enough information to tell us where their hearts stood before God.
External prosperity is not the same thing as spiritual prosperity.
A large family is not automatically a godly family.
A successful child is not automatically a surrendered child.
A respected household is not automatically a redeemed household.
And visible blessing should never be confused with saving grace.
That distinction becomes especially powerful in the book of Judges because Judges repeatedly shows us how desperately Israel needed more than another temporary human leader.
Again and again the pattern appears.
And the deeper human problem remains.
That difference leads us straight to Jesus Christ.
The judges could provide temporary deliverance.
Jesus provides the deliverance no earthly judge could accomplish.
The judges eventually died and remained among the dead.
The Gospel does not tell us that good people climb high enough to reach God.
The Gospel tells us that the Son of God came down to rescue sinners who could never save themselves.
Protected secret sins while maintaining respectable appearances.
Some of us learned how to look Christian long before we learned how to surrender.
We learned how to post Bible verses.
we also learned how to hide.
There are people reading this article who know exactly what that means.
Everyone thinks your marriage is fine.
Everyone thinks your faith is strong.
Everyone thinks that habit disappeared years ago.
It followed you into last night.
Jesus sees the room nobody else enters.
Not because sin does not matter.
Precisely because it matters so much that He went to the cross.
Jesus does not expose our sin merely to humiliate us.
He brings darkness into the light so sinners can repent, receive mercy, and become new.
The cross destroys two lies at once.
“Your sin is too terrible for Christ to forgive.”
Holy God receiving guilty people through the sacrifice of His sinless Son.
Not because they cleaned themselves first.
Maybe your family story is beautiful.
Maybe your mother disappeared emotionally when you needed her most.
Maybe your children barely speak to you.
Maybe addiction turned childhood memories into scars.
Maybe your surname carries pain instead of honor.
Maybe your family photographs contain people who no longer sit at the same table.
Maybe you look at Abdon's enormous household and do not feel impressed.
Your earthly family story does not get the final word over your identity.
The Gospel reaches into families filled with failure and begins creating something human effort could never manufacture.
New fathers who refuse to repeat what their fathers did.
New mothers who decide the cycle stops here.
Young men who choose holiness over secret pornography.
Young women who discover that their worth is not determined by whether somebody desires them.
Husbands who learn to repent instead of dominate.
Wives who learn to forgive without pretending sin is harmless.
Children who watch adults admit, “I was wrong. Please forgive me.”
Families opening Bibles where arguments once dominated every evening.
Maybe that is what someone in your family has been waiting to see.
We spend enormous energy asking what our children will inherit from us.
What are they learning from watching us suffer?
What do they see when we are angry?
Do they see humility when we are wrong?
Do they know we pray when nobody is watching?
Do they know that Jesus is more than the religious decoration hanging on our wall?
Do they see Christianity changing how we speak to people who cannot benefit us?
Because eventually your children may forget many of the things you purchased for them.
But they may remember hearing you pray their name before God.
They may remember the night you apologized.
They may remember seeing your Bible open before sunrise.
They may remember that when tragedy entered the house, your faith bent...
And perhaps years after you are gone, one of your grandchildren will repeat something you taught their parent about Jesus.
Suddenly Abdon's seventy descendants feel less like an ancient statistic.
But by God's grace, so can faithfulness.
And there is something else we desperately need to notice.
We often behave as though our current season is permanent.
Your influence has an expiration date.
Your career has an expiration date.
Your physical strength has an expiration date.
Your platform has an expiration date.
Your opportunity to tell certain people about Christ has an expiration date.
There will be a last conversation with your father.
A last meal with your mother.
A last time your child runs through your front door.
A last Sunday in your familiar church seat.
You probably will not know it is the last one while it is happening.
That is why the Gospel creates urgency without creating panic.
If there is someone you need to forgive, begin praying about it today.
If there is sin you need to confess, stop feeding it in darkness.
If you have wandered from Christ, return.
If your children have never heard your testimony, tell them what Jesus has done.
If someone you love does not know the Gospel, stop assuming there will always be another convenient opportunity.
And if you are reading this while carrying secret shame...
stop trying to rewrite your story without the Author.
Jesus can redeem what yesterday became.
You cannot crucify your own guilt away.
Christ already went to the cross.
You cannot resurrect your own heart.
But the risen Christ gives life.
This is why our message will always be:
Not because every earthly consequence disappears.
Not because repentance magically repairs every relationship overnight.
Not because following Jesus guarantees wealth, health, enormous families, or seventy donkeys.
The Gospel is infinitely better than that.
Jesus had no biological dynasty recorded like Abdon's.
Yet two thousand years later, men and women from nations Abdon never knew existed call Jesus Lord.
And the question is no longer merely what Abdon's enormous family tells us.
What will your life tell the people coming after you?
Will they inherit only your possessions?
Or will they inherit the memory of someone who loved Jesus?
Will your children remember Christianity as something you posted...
Will your grandchildren know you accumulated things...
or that you knew how to kneel?
And if you have no children at all, do not imagine that you have no spiritual legacy to leave.
A person online who almost scrolled past.
Faithfulness multiplies in ways we may never live long enough to see.
That is one reason Gospel-centered work matters.
When an article reaches a person at two in the morning who is ashamed to enter a church...
when a devotional reaches someone whose faith is collapsing...
when Scripture reaches a marriage in crisis...
when biblical truth reaches someone who has been discipled more by algorithms than by the Word of God...
we may never know on this side of eternity what God chooses to do with that seed.
And that is why, if Gospel Warrior has genuinely helped you grow closer to Christ, consider helping this ministry continue and expand.
The New Testament calls believers to generosity that is willing rather than coerced: “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” as Paul teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7.
But voluntary financial support of Gospel ministry can be a real act of Christian generosity and partnership.

So if God has given you the desire and ability to help Gospel Warrior keep producing Scripture-centered content, reaching more people, expanding discipleship resources, and pointing wounded and wandering hearts toward Jesus Christ, we would be deeply grateful for your monthly support.
The ashamed reminded that grace still has a name.
And financial support is not the only way you can help.
Sometimes one share reaches farther than money ever could.
Not simply to increase a number beneath a post, but because somebody connected to you may desperately need the message you almost kept to yourself.
Let them see that Christianity is not pretending Christians never fall.
It is the announcement that sinners can be forgiven because Jesus Christ died and rose again.
Come back to it when success starts convincing you that earthly accomplishments are permanent.
Come back when family disappoints you.
Come back when you are tempted to measure your life by possessions, followers, achievements, or applause.
Christ must be greater than all of it.
And if something inside you has been exposed while reading this, don't disappear silently.
And if you have been hiding something from God—as though anything could actually remain hidden from Him—perhaps your comment needs to be simpler still:
Let those words become more than engagement beneath an article.
Then take that decision somewhere deeper than a comment section.
Find mature believers who will walk with you.
Be part of a faithful local church.
Do not build your entire spiritual life around online content.
Online ministry can point you toward the Shepherd.
Never because someone implied God would love you more.
Never because you were promised earthly prosperity in return.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith”—not by building a dynasty, accumulating possessions, earning religious status, or financing a ministry.
We support Gospel work because we have already received something money could never purchase.
And maybe that is the secret hidden beneath Abdon's seventy riders.
Not a mystical meaning attached to the number seventy.
You can spend your entire life building something enormous...
and still eventually leave it behind.
So build what death cannot finally steal.
Carry the Gospel farther than your own lifetime.

And when your final chapter comes—and somebody else closes your eyes, empties your room, sorts through your possessions, and speaks your name in the past tense—may the greatest thing you leave behind not be what you owned.
May it be evidence that Jesus Christ owned your heart.
Because one day the donkeys disappear.
The houses belong to somebody else.
But the life surrendered to Jesus can leave fingerprints of grace on generations its owner never lived to meet.
